title: Section 1.6: Solving Linear Equations — Properties of Equality
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 11 • Section 1.6 (Workbook p. 18)
detail: Lecture 11: Properties of Equality & Multi-Term Equations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### The Golden Rule of Equation Solving
$$\text{Whatever you do to one side of the equation, you MUST do to the other side!}$$
- **Addition/Subtraction Property:** If $a = b$, then $a \pm c = b \pm c$.
- **Multiplication/Division Property:** If $a = b$ and $c \neq 0$, then $ac = bc$ and $\frac{a}{c} = \frac{b}{c}$.
- **Target Goal:** Isolate the variable term on one side and constants on the other.
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Simplify each side separately (distribute, combine like terms).} \\
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Use addition/subtraction to move variable terms to one side, numbers to other.} \\
\text{Step 3: } & \text{Multiply or divide by the variable's coefficient to get } x = \text{value}.
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Sora's Reminder:** An equation is a balance scale. Never alter one pan without altering the other!
script:
[Prof. Park] Welcome everyone to Lecture 11 of M090 Introductory Algebra! I am Professor Eunju Park, and joining me at the teaching desk is TA Sora.

[TA Sora] Today, we cross a major milestone in our course: we begin Section 1.6 on workbook pages 18 and 19: Solving Linear Equations and the Properties of Equality. Hello everyone! Up until today, we have been working with algebraic expressionsâsimplifying them, adding them, and multiplying them.

[Prof. Park] Notice that an expression has NO equal sign! You cannot solve an expression; you can only simplify it. Today, for the first time, we encounter an EQUATION: two algebraic expressions joined by an equal sign!

[TA Sora] An equation is a complete mathematical sentence that states: 'The left side has the EXACT same numerical value as the right side!'
That distinction is foundational.

[Prof. Park] Think of an equation as a traditional mechanical balance scale, like the antique gold and grain scales used during the Montana gold rush in Virginia City and Alder Gulch. If you have equal weights on both pans, the scale balances perfectly horizontally.

[TA Sora] If you add 5 pounds to the left pan, the scale tipsâunless you immediately add the exact same 5 pounds to the right pan!

[Prof. Park] That gives us our Golden Rule of Equation Solving: Whatever you do to one side of the equation, you MUST do to the other side! That is the universal law of algebra! Let's state our two core properties: 1.

[TA Sora] Addition and Subtraction Property of Equality: If a = b, then a + c = b + c, and a - c = b - c. Adding or subtracting the exact same number from both sides maintains complete equality. 2.

[Prof. Park] Multiplication and Division Property of Equality: If a = b and c is not zero, then a Â· c = b Â· c, and a / c = b / c. Multiplying or dividing both sides by the exact same non-zero number maintains complete equality.

[TA Sora] And what is our ultimate goal when solving an equation? Our goal is to isolate the variable completely by itself on one side: x = [a number].

[Prof. Park] To isolate the variable, we undo the operations that are attached to it using INVERSE operations in reverse order: Undo addition with subtraction; undo subtraction with addition; undo multiplication with division; and undo division with multiplication.

[TA Sora] Let's put this into practice on slide 2 with our first two-step equation! In the history of mathematics, the word 'algebra' comes from the 9th-century Arabic treatise 'Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala' by the Persian mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi.

[Prof. Park] The word 'al-jabr' literally meant 'the restoration of broken parts' or 'setting a broken bone'âre-balancing two sides of a scale! When an equation is out of balance, algebra provides the precise surgical operations to restore absolute equilibrium. That historical root is so inspiring!

[TA Sora] Whenever students ask me why algebra is so strict about doing the exact same thing to both sides, I tell them: think of flying a backcountry bush plane across the Absaroka Range.

[Prof. Park] If you load 50 pounds of survival gear onto the left wing, you MUST balance the aircraft by loading 50 pounds onto the right wing, or your plane will bank into the trees! Equations obey the exact same law of physical balance.

title: Example 1A: Two-Step Linear Equation
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 11 • Section 1.6 Example 1A (Workbook p. 18)
detail: Lecture 11: Properties of Equality & Multi-Term Equations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve the linear equation for the given variable (Workbook p. 18)
$$3x - 8 = -12$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Add } 8 \text{ to both sides to isolate the variable term:} \\
& 3x - 8 + 8 = -12 + 8 \\
& 3x = -4 \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Divide both sides by the coefficient } 3: \\
& \frac{3x}{3} = \frac{-4}{3} \\
& \mathbf{x = -\frac{4}{3}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Fraction Answers are Valid:** Many students panic when they get a fraction like $-\frac{4}{3}$ and think they made a mistake. In college algebra, fractions are authentic real numbers! Do not convert to rounded decimals!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 2, let's examine Section 1.6 Example 1A on workbook page 18: Solve the linear equation for the given variable: 3x - 8 = -12. Look at the variable x on the left side. What is happening to x?

[TA Sora] Two operations are attached to x: First, x is multiplied by 3. Second, 8 is subtracted from that result. When solving equations, we undo operations in REVERSE order of operationsâreverse PEMDAS! Think of getting dressed in the morning: you put your socks on first, then your boots.

[Prof. Park] When taking them off at night, what comes off first? The boots! So we undo the addition or subtraction first, and save the multiplication or division for the very last step! What a brilliant analogy, Sora!

[TA Sora] Let's take off the boots first: To undo the subtraction of 8, we add 8 to BOTH sides of the equation: 3x - 8 + 8 = -12 + 8. On the left side: -8 + 8 = 0, leaving just 3x.

[Prof. Park] On the right side: -12 + 8 = -4! So our equation simplifies to: 3x = -4. Now take off the socks: x is multiplied by 3. The inverse of multiplying by 3 is dividing by 3!

[TA Sora] Divide BOTH sides by 3: (3x) / 3 = (-4) / 3. 3 / 3 is 1, leaving x isolated: x = -4/3! Notice that our answer is an improper fraction in simplest form.

[Prof. Park] Do NOT convert it to a decimal like -1.333 unless the problem explicitly asks for a decimal. In algebra, -4/3 is exact, elegant, and standard.

[TA Sora] Now let's perform our mandatory check: plug x = -4/3 back into the original equation: 3(-4/3) - 8 = -4 - 8 = -12. -12 = -12 is a true statement! That proves with 100% mathematical certainty that x = -4/3 is the correct unique solution!

[Prof. Park] Let's discuss why we reverse the order of operations when solving equations. In Section 1.0, we learned PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication and Division, Addition and Subtraction. PEMDAS is for EVALUATING when you already know all the numbers and want to find the final value.

[TA Sora] Solving an equation is the exact REVERSE process: you already know the final value (-12), and you are working backward through time to discover what mystery number x created it! Exactly!

[Prof. Park] It's like wrapping a birthday gift: you put the toy in a box (multiplication), wrap it in paper (subtraction), and tie a bow. When unwrapping the gift, you don't break the toy firstâyou untie the bow, unwrap the paper (add 8), and open the box (divide by 3)!

[TA Sora] Reverse order of operations is the natural, logical unwrapping of an algebraic gift!

title: Example 1B: Negative Coefficient Trap
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 11 • Section 1.6 Example 1B (Workbook p. 18)
detail: Lecture 11: Properties of Equality & Multi-Term Equations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve the linear equation for the given variable (Workbook p. 18)
$$6 - 4w = 15$$
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{Step 1: } & \text{Subtract } 6 \text{ from both sides:} \\
& -4w = 15 - 6 \\
& -4w = 9 \\[0.8em]
\text{Step 2: } & \text{Divide both sides by } -4 \text{ (including the negative sign!):} \\
& \frac{-4w}{-4} = \frac{9}{-4} \\
& \mathbf{w = -\frac{9}{4}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **The Dropped Negative Sign:** Students often subtract 6 and write $4w = 9$, dropping the minus in front of $4w$. The term is $-4w$, so you MUST divide by $-4$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 3 introduces the notorious 'Negative Coefficient Trap': Section 1.6 Example 1B on workbook page 18: Solve: 6 - 4w = 15. Danger alert! Look at the left side: 6 - 4w. Students see the minus sign after 6 and mistakenly think the 6 is negative!

[TA Sora] They say: 'I should add 6 to both sides.' That is completely wrong! The number 6 has an invisible positive sign in front of it: +6! The minus sign belongs to the term 4w! So the coefficient of w is NEGATIVE 4!

[Prof. Park] That is one of the most common errors in all of introductory algebra. To eliminate the constant +6, we must SUBTRACT 6 from both sides: 6 - 4w - 6 = 15 - 6. On the left: 6 - 6 = 0, leaving -4w!

[TA Sora] Notice the minus sign did NOT disappearâit stays attached to 4w! On the right: 15 - 6 = 9. So our equation is: -4w = 9. Now to isolate w, we must divide both sides by the ENTIRE coefficient of w, which is -4!

[Prof. Park] Divide both sides by -4: (-4w) / (-4) = 9 / (-4). Negative divided by negative is positive: w = -9/4! If a student had forgotten that the 4 was negative, they would have divided by +4 and gotten +9/4, losing points.

[TA Sora] Always circle the sign in front of the coefficient to remind yourself that the sign travels with the number! Let's check w = -9/4: 6 - 4(-9/4) = 6 - (-9) = 6 + 9 = 15. 15 = 15! It checks out perfectly. Always guard your signs!

[Prof. Park] Here is an exam horror story from my first year as a TA: On a midterm question almost identical to 6 - 4w = 15, over 50% of the class wrote 4w = 9 instead of -4w = 9!

[TA Sora] They saw 6 - 4w and treated the minus sign like a decorative hyphen! A minus sign in algebra is never decorative! It is a negative charge that binds directly to the term immediately following it.

[Prof. Park] If you ever feel tempted to ignore that sign, rewrite the equation in standard form using the Commutative Property of Addition: -4w + 6 = 15! When you see -4w + 6 = 15, no one ever forgets that the 4 is negative!

[TA Sora] Rearranging terms to put the variable first is a bulletproof test-taking strategy.

title: Example 1C & 1D: Combining Like Terms First
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 11 • Section 1.6 Example 1C & 1D (Workbook p. 18)
detail: Lecture 11: Properties of Equality & Multi-Term Equations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Part\ C:}\quad & \text{Combine like terms on left side first:} \\
& (y + 5y) + (4 - 9) = 87 \implies 6y - 5 = 87 \\
& 6y = 87 + 5 = 92 \\
& y = \frac{92}{6} = \mathbf{\frac{46}{3}} \\[1em]
\mathbf{Part\ D:}\quad & \text{Combine like terms on left side:} \\
& (6r - 3r + 2r) + 94 = 18 \implies 5r + 94 = 18 \\
& 5r = 18 - 94 = -76 \\
& \mathbf{r = -\frac{76}{5}}
\end{aligned}$$
pitfall: **Reduce Fractions Fully:** In Part C, $\frac{92}{6}$ can both be divided by 2 to give $\frac{46}{3}$. Always simplify your final fraction!
script:
[Prof. Park] On slide 4, we examine Section 1.6 Examples 1C and 1D on workbook page 18: Equations where you must combine like terms on the same side BEFORE moving across the equal sign!

[TA Sora] Here is another vital distinction: If two like terms are on the SAME side of the equal sign, you do NOT use inverse operations! You simply combine them using regular addition and subtraction from Section 1.3!

[Prof. Park] You only use inverse operations when moving a term ACROSS the equal sign to the other side! Let's solve Example 1C: y + 4 + 5y - 9 = 87. Look at the left side: we have y and +5y.

[TA Sora] They are like terms! y + 5y = 6y. We also have constants +4 and -9: 4 - 9 = -5. So the left side simplifies to: 6y - 5 = 87. Look how simple that is now!

[Prof. Park] It's just a standard two-step equation: Add 5 to both sides: 6y = 87 + 5 = 92. Divide both sides by 6: y = 92/6. Both 92 and 6 are even numbers, so divide top and bottom by 2: y = 46/3! That is our simplified solution.

[TA Sora] Now let's solve Example 1D: 6r - 3r + 94 + 2r = 18. Combine all r terms on the left side: 6r - 3r = 3r, and 3r + 2r = 5r! So the left side becomes: 5r + 94 = 18.

[Prof. Park] Subtract 94 from both sides: 5r = 18 - 94 = -76. Divide both sides by 5: r = -76/5! 76 is not divisible by 5, so -76/5 is our final irreducible answer.

[TA Sora] Combining like terms first cuts the complexity of an equation in half before you ever touch an inverse operation!

[Prof. Park] Let's emphasize Sora's 'Border Crossing Rule' for slide 4: Look at Example 1C: y + 4 + 5y - 9 = 87. y and 5y are both on the left side of the border (the equal sign). Because they are on the same side, they don't need passports!

[TA Sora] You simply combine them: 1y + 5y = 6y! Students who try to subtract 5y from both sides here end up with a double-subtraction catastrophe! That's right! You only use inverse operations when crossing the international border of the equal sign!

[Prof. Park] If terms are inside the same country, just group them together normally like old friends. Organize your own house first before knocking on your neighbor's door!

title: Example 2A & 2B: Equations with Distributive Property
subtitle: Unit 1 • Lecture 11 • Section 1.6 Example 2A & 2B (Workbook p. 18)
detail: Lecture 11: Properties of Equality & Multi-Term Equations
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
### Solve each equation. Write answer in simplest fraction form (Workbook p. 18)
$$\text{A. } 10(a - 5) + 2 = -3$$
$$\text{B. } 6(x - 2) - 8 = 3x - 20$$
pitfall: **The Zero Solution Trap in 2B:** $x = 0$ is a VALID solution! Zero is a number! It does NOT mean 'no solution'!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 concludes Lecture 11 with Section 1.6 Examples 2A and 2B on workbook page 18: Solving Equations involving the Distributive Property. When an equation contains parentheses, our first priority is to eliminate parentheses using the Distributive Property.

[TA Sora] Let's look at Example 2A: 10(a - 5) + 2 = -3. Step 1: Distribute 10 across (a - 5): 10 Â· a - 10 Â· 5 = 10a - 50. So our equation is: 10a - 50 + 2 = -3.

[Prof. Park] Step 2: Combine like terms on the left side: -50 + 2 = -48. So we have: 10a - 48 = -3. Step 3: Add 48 to both sides: 10a = -3 + 48 = 45. Step 4: Divide both sides by 10: a = 45/10.

[TA Sora] Reduce by dividing top and bottom by 5: a = 9/2! Outstanding! Now let's tackle Example 2B, which has variables on BOTH sides of the equation: 6(x - 2) - 8 = 3x - 20.

[Prof. Park] Step 1: Distribute the 6 on the left: 6x - 12 - 8 = 3x - 20. Step 2: Combine like terms on the left: -12 - 8 = -20. So we get: 6x - 20 = 3x - 20. Step 3: Move variable terms to one side.

[TA Sora] Subtract 3x from both sides: 6x - 3x - 20 = -20, which gives: 3x - 20 = -20. Step 4: Add 20 to both sides: 3x = -20 + 20 = 0! Step 5: Divide both sides by 3: x = 0 / 3 = 0!

[Prof. Park] Students often freeze when they see zero and think something went wrong. Zero is a perfectly valid, real number! If x = 0, let's check: Left: 6(0 - 2) - 8 = 6(-2) - 8 = -12 - 8 = -20.

[TA Sora] Right: 3(0) - 20 = 0 - 20 = -20. -20 = -20! It checks completely. The solution is x = 0! In Lecture 12, we will look at equations where variables cancel out completelyâidentities and contradictions.

[Prof. Park] Great job today, and we look forward to seeing you in Lecture 12!

[TA Sora] In Example 2B, notice what happened when we reached 3x = 0: Many students panic and write: 'No solution' or 'Undefined.' Let's be 100% clear: 0 divided by 3 is ZERO: 0 / 3 = 0! Dividing zero by a number is completely legal and equals zero!

[Prof. Park] Dividing by zeroâlike 3 / 0âis what is undefined! Zero is a perfectly respectable integer! If the temperature outside in Bozeman during January drops to exactly 0Â° Fahrenheit, that does NOT mean the thermometer broke or that temperature has no solution! It means the temperature is zero!

[TA Sora] Always embrace x = 0 as a proud, valid solution!
